newsitem.title: USA: Equity transfer may constrain U.S. rural finances.
newsitem.headline: Equity transfer may constrain U.S. rural finances.

text.p: The aging rural population poses a challenge for rural lenders -- how to obtain capital for local lending when ownership of land and businesses passes to the Baby Boomers living in the city, speakers at a banking conference said Thursday.

"You have to ask what will happen to that money when it passes to the next generation," said Alan Tubbs, former president of the American Bankers Association, a U.S. trade group for the banking industry. "It's important for rural bankers to look for other sources of funding."

By some estimates, $7 billion-$10 billion in equity will change hands in the next decade through death and retirement. Speakers at the conference sponsored by the Kansas City Federal Reserve Bank said it was likely the money would leave rural areas. Baby Boomers also are more interested than their parents in mutual funds or other investments, rather than a savings account at a hometown bank, they said.

Kenneth Guenther, executive vice president of the Independent Bankers Associaton of America, a trade group representing locally-owned banks, said community banks were losing deposits to mutual funds, making liquidity a problem.
James Hansen, the Nebraska state banking director, also cited the approaching equity capital problem.
"We need additional sources of readily available credit" to back long-term loans, the Nebraska regulator said.

In the keynote speech for the conference, North Dakota State University professor Marvin Duncan referred to the problems of a declining deposit base and difficulty finding equity capital. But he also saw opportunity for rural economic growth because high-speed telecommunications made it possible for firms to locate far more of their operations in small towns.
